title: Florida Confirms First Burmese Python Breeding Population Outside the Everglades
excerpt: Wildlife officials say Charlotte County now hosts an established python population traced to released pets, with over three-fifths of sightings recorded since 2024.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Charlotte County is Florida's first established Burmese python population outside the Everglades.
  • Over three-fifths of 78 python sightings in Charlotte County occurred since 2024.
  • The population likely originated from escaped or released pets, not natural migration.
  • The 2026 Florida Python Challenge removed 294 pythons, with over 19,000 removed statewide since tracking began.

The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission has confirmed that Charlotte County, northwest of the Everglades, hosts the state's only known established Burmese python population beyond the Greater Everglades ecosystem. The finding marks a troubling new chapter in Florida's decades-long battle against one of its most destructive invasive species.

https://x.com/pbpost/status/2079642705248817547

Records from the Early Detection and Distribution Mapping System show 78 pythons have been captured, found dead or observed in Charlotte County. Over three-fifths of those sightings have been logged since 2024, according to the Palm Beach Post, pointing to a population that is growing, not shrinking.

Escaped Pets, Not Migration

FWC does not believe the Charlotte County snakes migrated naturally from the established Everglades population. Lisa Thompson, an FWC spokesperson, told the Palm Beach Post that "the FWC suspects that initially these animals were likely escaped or released captive animals."

Burmese pythons are currently considered established across a wide swath of southern Florida, from just south of Lake Okeechobee down to Key Largo and from western Broward County west to Collier County. Anything found outside that range has typically been classified as an escaped or released pet. Charlotte County's designation as an established population changes that calculus.

> **"Last year's event set a record with 294 pythons removed."**

An Apex Predator With Few Limits

Once they reach adulthood, Burmese pythons sit near the top of Florida's food chain. They prey on birds, mammals, reptiles, deer and even alligators, devastating native wildlife populations and reducing prey available to Florida panthers, bobcats and birds of prey.

"Once you have them out there and you have breeding populations, then your problem is far from over."

— Amy Kight, Chief Executive, Busch Wildlife Sanctuary

A single female can lay 50 to more than 100 eggs at a time. Scientists recently observed a Burmese python swallowing a 77-pound white-tailed deer, nearly 70 percent of the snake's own body mass. Conservative estimates by the U.S. Geological Survey put the Burmese python population in the Everglades region alone in the tens of thousands.

Stepped-Up Removal and a New Forecasting App

Officials have responded by increasing surveillance in Charlotte County. The FWC's Nonnative Fish and Wildlife Program hired two part-time python technicians in June 2024 to survey areas with the highest concentrations of snakes.

The 2026 Florida Python Challenge, which ran July 10 through 19, sent hundreds of professional and amateur hunters into eight South Florida hunting areas with $25,000 in cash prizes at stake. Last year's event set a record with 294 pythons removed. Since statewide removal programs began, more than 19,000 Burmese pythons have been taken out of Florida's landscape.

Meanwhile, University of Florida researchers are developing a python forecasting app that would use years of removal data to predict the best times and locations for hunts. The app draws on a study published in the journal Scientific Reports that analyzed 16,000 hours of hunting data and found that the optimal hunting window is between 8 p.m. and 2 a.m. during the May-to-October wet season, with August yielding the highest catch rates.

Climate Change and the Road Ahead

Researchers worry that warming temperatures could expand the areas where Burmese pythons can survive in Florida. That concern deepened in 2023 when the U.S. Department of Agriculture updated its plant hardiness zones, shifting much of the state into warmer categories.

For Florida's large Indian diaspora, concentrated in cities like Orlando, Tampa, Jacksonville and Miami, the python crisis is more than an environmental curiosity. The invasive species disrupts ecosystems tied to recreation, tourism and property values across the state.

Wildlife officials urge anyone who spots a Burmese python to report it to the FWC's Invasive Species Hotline at 888-Ive-Got1 or through the IveGot1 mobile app. Experts caution against attempting to handle large snakes without experience.
